episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Wild Spaces & Outdoor Life
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Wild Spaces & Outdoor Life.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Who decides what's worth saving?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [My Cariboo Now] Police in 100 Mile House respond to road rage incident and [My Cariboo Now] Quesnel is getting ready to take back the night, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Should provincial prescribed burn decisions be made unilaterally by BC Wildfire Service, or should Indigenous Nations have co-decision authority over land management in their territories? Topics include: Indigenous co-decision authority versus consultation in land management, Scientific evidence and limitations of prescribed burning effectiveness, Climate intensification (El Niño patterns) and local mitigation actions, Comparison of Indigenous-led burning versus provincial protocols and timelines, Governance structures and liability frameworks shaping wildfire prevention decisions.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Chilcotin Conservation Society

discussion.central_question: Should provincial prescribed burn decisions be made unilaterally by BC Wildfire Service, or should Indigenous Nations have co-decision authority over land management in their territories?
discussion.riley_position: Prescribed burning is necessary fire management grounded in solid science and Indigenous agreement on the principle of fire; the real question is ensuring meaningful consultation happens and governance processes improve, but waiting for perfect evidence while fuel loads build carries its own worse consequences.
riley_key_evidence: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center flagged greater-than-90% probability of very strong El Niño events recurring more intensely than historical baseline
BC Wildfire Service has consultation protocols with Nations built into burn planning, which represents real improvement over no coordination
Summerland evacuated for 25 straight days last summer, showing real wildfire risk from unmanaged interior forest
discussion.casey_position: The Deer Park burn represents a colonial extraction of Indigenous burning techniques without transferring decision-making authority; the province is advancing a 450-hectare burn based on unsettled science while excluding Indigenous Nations from actual control over land management decisions.
casey_key_evidence: 2024 peer-reviewed study found prescribed fires under certain conditions actually raised probability of subsequent wildfire rather than lowering it
2025 People and Nature journal paper shows prescribed burning only works in specific contexts, yet agencies routinely stretch evidence beyond where it holds
Kanaka Bar's goat program demonstrates Indigenous-led fuel reduction on its own timeline and authority, contrasting sharply with ministry-scheduled burns
discussion.resolution: Riley and Casey agreed on a concrete test case: whether the Cariboo Regional District or Nations with territory touching planned burns secure formal co-decision authority (not just consultation) in burn planning before next spring fire season; they set this as the measurable marker to determine if reconciliation is substantive or theatrical.
